a.xlink:title: `/shared` is what makes RWX unavoidable, but homes are the larger prize. Nothing in the pack's contract requires RWX for a home volume; what recommends it is that RWX homes dissolve the per-user node pin, the cross-AZ constraint, and Longhorn's presence on AWS in one move rather than mitigating each separately. So the capability is forced by `/shared` and wanted well beyond it — see Topic: home volume access mode for the full argument and the performance evidence against it. Cross-pack sharing is a third candidate, where no requirement is established at all and object storage may serve it instead.

a.xlink:title: Nebari has no AWS identity per Keycloak user and no secrets-management system — one IAM identity deploys the cluster, and JupyterLab pods carry no AWS credentials (Marcelo Villa, 2026-08-13). Group-scoped access would mean mapping Keycloak groups onto IAM policy or bucket prefixes, which Marcelo called a mess that arrives quickly. Mounting a bucket as a filesystem (goofys-style) makes the paths look normal but moves none of this.

a.xlink:title: Reach for object storage rather than RWX in any scenario it can serve, and treat a shared filesystem as the fallback for what genuinely needs POSIX. Stated as a working preference (James Olds, 2026-08-14), not a team decision, and it cuts hardest at cross-pack sharing, where no RWX requirement has been established at all. Its own costs are unsettled and named in Object storage changes the product contract: no per-user AWS identity to key access on, unproven small-file and metadata performance, and no in-cluster option short of running MinIO or equivalent — which trades the managed service for another storage system to operate.

a.xlink:title: Nebari should standardize the RWX capability and its acceptance criteria while allowing each infrastructure provider to supply the most suitable implementation.

The 2026-08-13 discussion added three more adverse data points, each qualified by the person raising it. Tyler Potts: EFS caps IOPS where S3 parallelises reads across Ray workers, and EFS can get expensive. Nick Byrne: data-engineering reads are metadata-heavy — a Parquet sidecar read repeatedly to skip irrelevant blobs — which is where EFS is said to degrade, but he flagged it explicitly as inherited folklore he has never tested. Vini Cerutti: Quansight benchmarked blob storage against EFS and concluded EFS was too slow, and Confluency moved off EFS to S3 for exactly that Parquet read/write pattern — but that is three to four years old and Nebari Classic era. None of it measures Elastic throughput mode, and none of it is about FSx for OpenZFS.

a.xlink:title: The single-writer ordering does not survive load. From one to four concurrent writers Longhorn degrades 2.2-2.6x and FSx 1.7-2.7x, while EFS Elastic is flat (1.1-1.2x) — so by four writers the three converge and EFS is fastest on environment creation (72 s, against Longhorn 83 s and FSx 99 s). The mechanism is structural: Longhorn funnels every client through one share-manager pod on one node and FSx is capped by its provisioned throughput tier, both fixed budgets divided among clients, where EFS scales capacity on demand. Nebari is a multi-user platform and four writers is a small cluster; where the crossover sits beyond four is unmeasured and is the most decision-relevant gap left in the performance evidence.

a.xlink:title: Longhorn remains necessary for providers that lack a suitable managed RWX abstraction.

At one writer Longhorn RWX matches FSx on extraction, clone and checkout and is 1.8x faster on environment creation (32.0 s against 56.3 s). Moving `/shared` to a managed filesystem is therefore a measurable regression on the workload the pack cares most about — the map already says a managed filesystem buys operational simplification rather than speed, and that is now confirmed with a price attached rather than assumed to be zero. The advantage inverts under concurrency, per concurrency inverts the ranking.

a.xlink:title: Longhorn holds several roles in NIC at once — sole default StorageClass, RWX implementation, and backup implementation — and it was adopted for none of them: ADR-0002 adopted it for the cross-AZ attach problem, with RWX and backups named as benefits that came later. The roles arrived separately and are separable, so the default-class one is decidable on its own, whichever way the AWS question goes.

The honest unit of Longhorn's operational cost is per cluster and per operator, not per provider. Removing it from AWS does not remove it from the project while Hetzner needs it, but it does remove it from every AWS cluster and everyone on call for one. Priced under the operations gate.

a.xlink:title: The cost gate asks for operator overhead as a line item inside it, and the unit is hours per cluster per month because that is how the burden scales. Built from the runbooks NIC ships and the incidents observed during the benchmark — drains and node maintenance ~3 h, incident response ~2 h, upgrades, capacity tuning, backup drift checks and maintaining the expertise — Longhorn totals ~9.3 h/mo against ~2.3 h/mo residual on a managed filesystem, a delta of ~7 h/mo/cluster. It is left in hours on purpose: converting it needs a loaded rate, and whoever owns the staffing budget has that rate. Two consequences do not need one — the delta is flat, so ten Longhorn clusters is ~70 h/mo, roughly half an FTE; and being flat it weighs heaviest on small clusters, where the whole infrastructure bill is $231/mo. This is an estimate, not a measurement, and it is the number most worth firming up: tag storage-related toil in on-call's tracker for a quarter. It is here because leaving it out prices it at zero, which is the one value known to be wrong.

a.xlink:title: Getting the benchmark cluster into a testable state hit the drain problem directly (2026-08-14). A routine node-group disk resize on `jamesolds-dev` failed three times, roughly 29 minutes each, with `PodEvictionFailure`: Longhorn's `instance-manager` PDB reported zero allowed disruptions while it held a volume's last replica, under the default `node-drain-policy: block-if-contains-last-replica`. Neither surge headroom nor detaching the workload cleared it, and the roll completed only with `--force`. So routine node maintenance on a Longhorn cluster means deliberately relaxing a data-safety setting first, which is the runbook's five steps meeting a real cluster. Two adjacent findings came with it: `max_nodes` must exceed `min_nodes` or an EKS node-group update has no room to launch a replacement before draining, which makes any PDB unsatisfiable (worth a NIC validation, and independent of Longhorn); and `keycloak-db-primary` sits at zero allowed disruptions too, so the cluster has a second, unrelated reason a node cannot be drained — relevant to HA is not durability and to the CNPG `instances: 2-3` discussion. The `max_nodes` gap is a NIC validation we will add, and the drain procedure can be automated further than it is — but the burden itself survives both fixes, because what the operator is doing is evicting replicas from a storage system whose safety setting has to be relaxed for maintenance to proceed. Better tooling shortens that; it does not remove the class of work.

a.xlink:title: Longhorn keeps replicas under `/var/lib/longhorn` on the node root disk and reserves 25% of it, so NIC's 20 GB default leaves ~2.4 GB schedulable. A 20 GiB RWX volume therefore goes straight to `faulted`/`detached`, no share-manager pod is created, and consuming pods sit in `ContainerCreating` until they time out, with no error naming disk space (observed 2026-08-14; fixed by setting `disk_size: 100`). RWX is the only capability Longhorn is retained for on AWS under the split shape, and it is broken on a default-shaped cluster. This is a NIC bug and will be fixed in NIC — raise the default when Longhorn is enabled, or fail validation up front — so it is not an argument that Longhorn cannot work here. What it is evidence of is how much Longhorn-specific knowledge the integration silently assumes: the failure names no cause, and diagnosing it means knowing about the 25% reserve on `/var/lib/longhorn`.

It should be costed as a do-nothing-else alternative before either migration is proposed.

a.xlink:title: Replica capacity lives on the node root disk and gp3 caps at 16 TiB per volume, so the 66.7 TiB raw a 200-user tier needs cannot sit on the 2-3 storage nodes the example configs imply — it needs at least five, purely as an EBS volume-size constraint that nothing in NIC computes or checks. Each of those volumes also gets gp3's baseline 125 MBps regardless of size, and NIC's `node_groups` schema cannot express gp3 IOPS or throughput at all, so a Longhorn storage backplane is capped there with no config path to raise it. That is very likely a second, independent ceiling behind the measured 2.2-2.6x concurrency degradation, alongside the share-manager funnel — and the cheaper one to fix. All of it is fixable in NIC and will be; the point is that scaling Longhorn correctly is knowledge the platform currently expects the operator to supply.

a.xlink:title: The cost model gives the other half of concurrency inverts the ranking. EFS storage is 3.3x FSx Single-AZ ($0.30 vs $0.09/GB-mo) and its Elastic mode bills data access per GB — $0.03 read, $0.06 write — with no ceiling, so at 500 GB read plus 100 GB write per user per month it reaches $7,300/mo at the large tier, worse than Longhorn. So the trade is explicit: EFS buys flat concurrency scaling with a variable bill, FSx buys a fixed bill with a throughput ceiling. Neither the benchmark nor the cost model measures actual GB/user/month, so the EFS figure is a sensitivity range spanning 3.4x rather than a price, and getting that number from a live cluster is the second-biggest gap in the costing. The same unmodelled per-operation charge applies to FSx Multi-AZ Intelligent-Tiering, which is otherwise 8x cheaper than provisioned SSD — on a workload the benchmark showed to be metadata-operation-bound, which is the most likely way these numbers are wrong in the cheap direction.

a.xlink:title: The volume stays where it is either way; what per-AZ node groups (or Karpenter) buy is that "give me a node in this specific AZ" becomes an answerable request, so a rescheduled pod comes back as soon as its AZ has capacity — and when the AZ is what failed, it comes back with the AZ, rather than sitting in a pending state that reads like a storage bug. That is a documented topology fix, not a storage-layer one. The honest residual: if that AZ itself is gone, EBS-backed volumes are stranded until it returns, where Longhorn would usually reattach from a surviving replica — a real, priceable availability trade, not a blocker.

a.xlink:title: The fix is documented but not free. One node group per AZ multiplies the node-group config surface by the number of zones — scaling bounds, instance types, taints, labels, and GPU variants replicated per zone — and each group scales independently, so headroom is per-AZ and utilisation drops. Karpenter avoids the fan-out by reading the PV's zone requirement natively, but replaces cluster-autoscaler, which is its own migration. Neither is exotic; both are more configuration than the single multi-AZ ASG NIC ships today, and that delta belongs in the comparison rather than in a footnote.

a.xlink:title: The residual is an availability trade, and its size depends on how often AZs fail and for how long. Full-AZ outages are infrequent and typically measured in hours, recovery needs no operator action — the volumes are intact and the pods reschedule when capacity returns — and the workload is interactive analysis rather than a customer-facing service, where the tolerable answer may simply be that affected users cannot work until the AZ is back. Two things keep this from being free: Nebari has no stated availability objective to check it against, so "acceptable" is currently a preference rather than a finding; and the services that genuinely should survive a lost AZ are databases, which the anecdotes do not transfer puts on CNPG replication rather than on the storage layer. Note also that Longhorn's own survival here is softer than assumed — NIC sets replica zone anti-affinity to soft with two replicas, so both can sit in the AZ that just failed.

a.xlink:title: The RWX-homes shape dissolves the objection rather than answering it: FSx for OpenZFS Multi-AZ presents a floating endpoint with automatic failover to a standby in a second AZ (EFS is regional with a mount target per AZ and shares the property), so a home is reachable from any AZ, there is no AZ to be pinned to, and an AZ outage becomes AWS's failover problem rather than the cluster's. The 2026-08-14 benchmark prices that: Multi-AZ costs about 20% over Single-AZ on extraction and clone, nothing on environment creation, and the two are indistinguishable at four writers — so cross-AZ write acknowledgement is not what constrains FSx, its throughput tier is. The dissolution is cheap in latency and not cheap in dollars: Multi-AZ is 1.65-1.67x Single-AZ on the bill (2x storage, 3.3x throughput), so the cross-AZ guarantee moves from a performance question to a cost one — whether AZ-outage availability for `/shared` is worth about $285/mo at the medium tier is a product question nobody has been asked. And the shape still has the adverse home-gate numbers to answer regardless.

a.xlink:title: A measurement only decides something against a stated bar, and nobody has said what environment-rebuild or `git checkout` latency is acceptable. A minute for an occasional environment build may be a perfectly good price for free scheduling, no AZ pin, and one less storage system to operate; 15-32 s for a branch switch several times an hour is a different proposition, and the numbers cannot separate them on their own. The gp3 re-baseline is now done, so the one thing outstanding is the ceiling itself, and it is a product conversation rather than a measurement.

a.xlink:title: On a block volume the kubelet sets ownership: `fsGroup: 100` with `fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch` makes the volume root group-owned so the container's non-root user can write. NFS-backed CSI drivers report no fsGroup support, so the kubelet skips that step and a freshly provisioned export arrives owned by whoever the appliance created it as — typically root — with the user unable to write to their own home. A dedicated per-user volume does not fix this by itself: nothing chowns it. What fixes it is the appliance doing the job instead — FSx for OpenZFS takes root uid/gid and permissions as volume-creation parameters, and controls root-squash; EFS uses access points that force a POSIX user on every request. So this is solvable per user, and the point is only that it is a different mechanism, configured in StorageClass parameters rather than in the pod spec, and therefore has to be verified rather than assumed to carry over. The reason the POSIX behavior gate names fsGroup explicitly.

a.xlink:title: Longhorn leaves AWS entirely is not distinct to the RWX-homes shape. The cost model's favoured shape — homes RWO on gp3 with only `/shared` on a managed filesystem — also removes Longhorn from AWS, and costs less. What RWX homes distinctly buy is the end of the per-user node pin and of the AZ binding; what the gp3 shape pays instead is the cross-AZ topology work of Assumption 15. So the dissolves-several-problems argument overstates its margin by one: the comparison that matters is pin-plus-AZ against the 9-37x write penalty, with Longhorn's departure common to both sides.
